case.title: Venue recording: was the camera clock right?
case.brief: An 18-minute phone video filmed indoors at a hackathon venue on Sunday 8 November 2026. The file says it started at 11:42:37 UTC. Independently establish when it was really recorded, without trusting the file's clock.

claim.description: File metadata says recording started 2026-11-08 11:42:37 UTC (UK time = UTC in November).

text: Static tripod-style shot of strip ceiling lights, no windows/daylight, no on-screen clock. Light flicker is strong (18 dB, 67% usable); audio hum is weak (17% usable) — use video.

input.headline: The power-grid pattern recorded by the ceiling lights shows this video started at about 11:42:39 UTC on 8 November 2026. That is within 2 seconds of the time in the file, so the phone's clock was right.
input.difference: 2 seconds, which is within the method's precision of about ±5 seconds. In practice there is no difference.
findings: The scene is a fixed view of strip ceiling lights indoors. There are no windows and no clock on screen, so the lights are the only timing evidence in the picture.

The lights flicker with the mains supply, and that flicker came through strongly: about two-thirds of the 18 minutes was usable. The mains hum in the sound was weak (17% usable), probably drowned out by people talking, so I used only the lights.
No 1-second national grid record is available for November 2026, so I compared the video against Elexon's grid record, which has one reading every 15 seconds.
Searching 08:00 to 16:00 UTC on 8 Nov found the best match at 11:42:39 with a score of 0.98 (1.0 is a perfect match). The next-best time that day scored only 0.84.
Other days: the best match on any day from 5 to 11 Nov scored 0.84. That makes a recording on another day very unlikely.
Each half of the video, checked separately, points to the same start time to within 1 second. This fits one continuous recording and gives no sign of editing or joined clips.
The match gets steadily worse when the start time is moved away from 11:42:39 (0.70 at one minute off). The timing is precise to within a few seconds.
input.what_it_means: The pattern of tiny mains-frequency changes captured in the video fits only one time slot on the national record: 11:42:39 UTC on Sunday 8 November 2026. This finding does not rely on the phone's clock or the file's metadata, and it agrees with them. The file's start time can be relied on to within a few seconds. The checks found no sign that the footage comes from another day or was cut and joined.
next_steps: You can treat the file's time stamp (11:42:37 UTC, which is also UK local time) as independently confirmed to within about ±5 seconds.
If someone disputes it, you could re-check the match against the NESO record, which has one reading per second, once November 2026 is published. That would tighten the precision.
This result tells you when the video was made. It does not tell you where, or who made it. Confirm the venue by other means if that matters.
